title: Scatterplots, correlation and trend lines
blurb: Name a correlation's direction and strength, predict with a trend line, and know why correlation does not prove causation.
question: A scatterplot of 9 nursing applicants shows weekly study hours (x) against practice test scores (y). The points rise from lower left to upper right and sit close to the trend line y = 3x + 52. What kind of correlation is this, what score does the line predict for 6.5 hours, and can you conclude that studying caused the higher scores?

teach.h: One dot per person, two numbers per dot
teach.body: Formally, a scatterplot graphs paired numerical data: each point (x, y) records two variables measured on the same individual, and the overall pattern shows the correlation between them. In plain English: every dot is one person (or day, or patient), placed across by one measurement and up by the other. You don't read single dots so much as the shape of the whole cloud: does it rise, fall or do nothing?

teach.h: Positive correlation: study hours and scores
teach.caption: Dots rise from lower left to upper right and hug the trend line y = 3x + 52: a strong positive correlation.

teach.h: Three directions a scatterplot can take
Strength: how tightly the dots hug a line
teach.body: Direction says which way the cloud slopes; strength says how closely the dots follow a straight line. Dots packed tightly along a line show a strong correlation; dots spread widely around a general slope show a weak one. A strong negative correlation is just as strong as a strong positive one. It is a real relationship, not 'no relationship.' A lone dot far from the pattern is an outlier.

teach.h: Negative correlation: exercise and resting heart rate
teach.caption: As exercise hours go up, resting heart rate tends to go down. The dots stay close to the line, so this is a strong negative correlation.

teach.h: Scenario: Danielle predicts with the trend line
items: Danielle Kim surveys 9 classmates (study hours 2 to 10) and draws the trend line y = 3x + 52.
6.5 hours lies inside the data (2 to 10 hours), so this is interpolation: a reasonable estimate.
Predict for 25 hours: 3 × 25 + 52 = 127, a score above the 100 maximum. Extrapolating far beyond the data gives nonsense.

teach.body: A correlation shows that two variables move together, not that one causes the other. A third variable can drive both: towns with more fire trucks have more fires, because bigger towns have more of both. In Danielle's survey, students with more study hours may also have more free time or a stronger science background. Only a controlled experiment can show cause and effect.

teach.text: Classic slips: calling a strong negative correlation 'no relationship'; concluding 'x causes y' from a scatterplot; trusting a prediction far outside the data range; and swapping the axes, so the variable on the y-axis is treated as the input.

items: Each point is one individual's (x, y) pair; read the overall pattern.
Positive: rises left to right. Negative: falls. None: a shapeless cloud.
Strong = dots hug the line; weak = dots spread widely around it.
Predict by substituting x into the trend line; trust predictions inside the data range.
Correlation is not causation: look for a third variable.

summary: You can now describe a scatterplot's correlation by direction and strength, predict values by substituting into a trend line, and judge when a prediction is trustworthy. You also know that a correlation alone never proves that one variable causes the other.

A.q: A scatterplot shows daily sodium intake (x) and systolic blood pressure (y) for 25 adults. The points rise from lower left to upper right, but they are spread widely around that general upward direction. Which best describes the relationship?
A.why: Rising from lower left to upper right means positive. Points spread widely around the trend mean the correlation is weak.

whyNot.1: A strong correlation needs the points packed tightly along a line; these are spread widely.
whyNot.2: Negative correlations fall from upper left to lower right; these points rise.
whyNot.3: There is a clear upward direction, so there is some correlation.

A.q: Data from 50 US cities show a strong positive correlation between the number of fast-food restaurants and the number of hospital beds. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Fast food causes the extra hospital beds
Adding beds attracts more fast-food outlets
Both may rise with a city's population
The two counts have no real relationship
A.why: Correlation does not show causation. A third variable, population size, would raise both counts, which fits a strong positive correlation without either causing the other.

whyNot.0: A correlation cannot show that one variable causes the other.
whyNot.1: This also claims causation, just in the reverse direction, which the data cannot show.
whyNot.3: A strong positive correlation is a real statistical relationship, even though it is not causal.

A.q: On a scatterplot of weekly exercise hours (x) and resting heart rate in beats per minute (y), the trend line is y = −1.5x + 78. What resting heart rate does the line predict for 6 hours of exercise per week?

whyNot.1: 78 − 6 = 72 subtracts the hours without multiplying by the slope.
whyNot.2: 78 − 1.5 = 76.5 uses the slope once instead of multiplying it by 6.
whyNot.3: 78 + 9 = 87 drops the negative sign on the slope.

B.q: Which pair of variables would most likely show a negative correlation?
B.why: As a car gets older, its resale value tends to fall: one variable rises while the other falls, which is a negative correlation.

whyNot.0: Taller adults tend to have larger feet, a positive correlation.
whyNot.1: More hours worked means more pay, a positive correlation.
whyNot.2: Birth month has no link to test scores: no correlation.

B.q: Scatterplot P has points packed tightly along a line that falls from left to right. Scatterplot Q has points loosely spread around a band that rises from left to right. Which description is correct?
options: P strong negative; Q weak positive
P weak negative; Q strong positive
P strong positive; Q weak negative
P strong negative; Q no correlation
B.why: Tight along a falling line = strong negative. Loosely spread around a rising band = weak positive.

whyNot.1: This swaps the strengths: P's tight points make it the strong one.
whyNot.2: This swaps the directions: P falls (negative) and Q rises (positive).
whyNot.3: Q has a clear rising direction, so it shows a weak positive correlation, not none.

B.q: A scatterplot of children aged 2 to 10 has the trend line h = 2.5a + 31, where h is height in inches and a is age in years. Which prediction from this line is least reliable?
B.why: Age 30 is far outside the data (2 to 10 years). Extrapolating predicts 106 inches, almost 9 feet, because children's growth does not continue at the same rate.

whyNot.0: Age 4 lies inside the data range, so 2.5 × 4 + 31 = 41 inches is a reasonable interpolation.
whyNot.1: Age 7.5 lies inside the data range: 2.5 × 7.5 + 31 = 49.75 inches.
whyNot.2: Age 10 is the edge of the data, still inside the range: 2.5 × 10 + 31 = 56 inches.

C.q: A scatterplot of patients' daily steps in thousands (x) and fasting glucose in mg/dL (y) has the trend line y = −3x + 110. What does the −3 mean?
options: Glucose is about 3 at zero steps a day
Steps fall about 3,000 per glucose unit
Walking causes glucose to drop by 3
C.why: The slope is the change in y per 1-unit change in x. One unit of x is 1,000 steps, so each extra 1,000 steps goes with glucose about 3 mg/dL lower.

whyNot.0: The value at zero steps is the y-intercept, 110, not the slope.
whyNot.1: This swaps the variables: the slope is change in y per unit of x.
whyNot.3: A trend line from observational data shows correlation, not causation.

C.q: A trend line on a scatterplot of study hours (x) and practice scores (y) passes through the points (2, 58) and (10, 82). What score does the line predict for 7 hours of study?
C.why: Slope = (82 − 58) ÷ (10 − 2) = 24 ÷ 8 = 3 points per hour. From (2, 58), 7 hours is 5 hours more: 58 + 3 × 5 = 73.

whyNot.0: 59.7 uses run over rise (8 ÷ 24 = 0.33) as the slope.
whyNot.1: 70 divides 24 by 10 (the second x-value) instead of the change in x, 8.
whyNot.3: 79 adds 3 × 7 to 58, as if 58 were the score at 0 hours rather than at 2.

C.q: A survey of 200 teens finds a strong negative correlation between screen time before bed and hours of sleep. Which conclusion is supported?
options: Screen time causes teens to lose sleep
Teens who sleep less have less screen time
Screen time and sleep are not related
More screen time goes with less sleep
C.why: A negative correlation means that as one variable rises the other tends to fall, so more screen time goes with less sleep. A survey cannot show which, if either, causes the other.

whyNot.0: This claims causation, which a correlation cannot establish.
whyNot.1: This describes a positive correlation (both low together), the opposite direction.
whyNot.2: A strong negative correlation is a clear relationship, not 'no relationship.'

reteach.title: Footprints in the sand
reteach.question: Footprints on a beach rise in size as they get closer to the lifeguard tower. Does that mean the tower makes feet grow? What do footprints teach you about scatterplots?

blocks.body: Imagine each footprint is a dot. If bigger prints sit nearer the tower, there's a pattern: a correlation. But maybe adults walk to the tower and children stay by the water. The pattern is real; the cause is something else (age). Scatterplots work the same way. The direction of the cloud tells you how the two measurements move together. It never tells you why.

blocks.h: No correlation: birth month and height
blocks.caption: A shapeless cloud with a flat trend line: knowing someone's birth month tells you nothing about their height.

blocks.text: Before you say 'x causes y,' ask: could a third variable (like age, population or weather) push both up or down together?

explain.body: Read the cloud left to right. Rising means positive (as x increases, y tends to increase). Falling means negative (as x increases, y tends to decrease). No slope means no correlation.

test.q: A nurse records pairs (x, y) for six patients: (1, 9), (2, 8), (3, 8), (4, 6), (5, 5), (6, 3). Plotted as a scatterplot, what correlation do the points show?
test.why: As x increases from 1 to 6, y falls steadily from 9 to 3, with every point close to a straight falling line: a strong negative correlation.

whyNot.0: The y-values fall as x rises, so the correlation is negative, not positive.
whyNot.2: The points fall, and they follow the line closely, so this is neither positive nor weak.
whyNot.3: There is a clear, steady downward pattern.

explain.body: Strength is how closely the dots follow a straight line, whatever its direction. Tight = strong; widely spread = weak. Positive and negative correlations can be equally strong.

test.q: Two scatterplots both slope upward. In plot P the dots lie almost exactly on a line; in plot Q they spread widely around a rising band. Which statement is correct?
options: P and Q are equally strong
test.why: Strength depends on how tightly the dots follow a line. P's dots lie almost on the line, so P is stronger.

whyNot.0: Q's dots are widely spread, which makes its correlation weaker.
whyNot.2: Sharing a direction does not mean sharing a strength.
whyNot.3: Q slopes upward, so its correlation is positive.

explain.body: Substitute the x-value into the line's equation and calculate y. Predictions inside the data range (interpolation) are reasonable; far outside it (extrapolation) they can be absurd.

steps.label: Check the x-range
steps.sub: Is the x-value inside the data?

steps.label: Substitute
steps.sub: y = mx + b with your x

test.q: A scatterplot of practice questions answered per week (x, from 20 to 120) and practice score (y) has the trend line y = 0.2x + 58. What score does the line predict for 90 questions a week?

whyNot.0: 58.2 adds the slope to the intercept and leaves out x.
whyNot.3: 148 adds 90 to 58 without multiplying by the slope.

explain.body: Two variables can move together because a third variable drives both, or by coincidence. A scatterplot shows association; only a controlled experiment can show cause.

test.q: A town notices that months with higher ice cream sales also have more sunburn cases at its clinic. What is the best explanation?
options: Sunburn makes people crave ice cream
The two counts are not related
test.why: Hot, sunny weather is a third variable that increases both ice cream sales and sunburns, producing the correlation without either causing the other.

whyNot.0: A correlation cannot show that ice cream causes sunburn.
whyNot.2: This reverses the causal claim but is still causation inferred from correlation.
whyNot.3: The counts are related: they rise together, which is a positive correlation.
